claims.text: CuMoTaWV is a refractory high-entropy alloy suitable for film deposition.
Post-deposition annealing under controlled conditions creates a continuous, uniform nanocrystalline oxide layer on CuMoTaWV films.
As-sputtered CuMoTaWV films have no pre-existing protective oxide layer.
An optional pre-oxidation step can help guarantee uniform nanocrystalline oxide formation.
The annealing-induced oxide layer chemically passivates the CuMoTaWV substrate against corrosive agents.
The annealing-induced oxide layer has low-friction behavior.
The annealing-induced oxide layer is sufficiently hard to reduce mechanical material removal.
The combination of passivation, low friction, and high hardness synchronously mitigates wear and corrosion.
The dual-function oxide layer governs the simultaneous wear-corrosion resistance of CuMoTaWV films under harsh environments.
Optimally annealed CuMoTaWV films will have a lower coefficient of friction than non-annealed films.
Optimally annealed CuMoTaWV films will have lower wear volume than non-annealed films.
Optimally annealed CuMoTaWV films will have lower corrosion rates than non-annealed films.
Samples with non-uniform oxide layers will exhibit degradation similar to the untreated baseline.
The predicted protection should operate near 300 °C in an oxidizing saline atmosphere under cyclic mechanical loading.
The oxide-mediated protection may provide no significant improvement in milder environments.
Failure to form a uniform oxide layer may eliminate the predicted protection.
Variation in oxide thickness, grain size, and uniformity may produce localized differences in degradation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts that non-uniform oxide coverage should cause baseline-like or locally high degradation, but the falsification rule treats non-uniform coverage correlated with high degradation as falsifying the hypothesis. That observation would instead agree with the stated mediator and boundary condition.

The boundary allows annealed samples to show no improvement when a uniform oxide fails to form, whereas the falsification rule treats lack of improvement in annealed samples as falsifying without explicitly requiring confirmation that the intended uniform oxide was successfully formed.
